questions.question: A team moves a coding assistant that worked well through claude -p into a Python service built on the Claude Agent SDK, where engineers still watch and steer its repository work. With no system prompt configured, the agent has lost the tool-usage habits and safety behavior the CLI showed. What should the developer do?

options.text: Write a short custom system prompt describing the agent's role, since a custom string keeps the CLI's guidance underneath
Load the project setting sources so the SDK picks up the Claude Code system prompt from the repository
Start from the Claude Code preset system prompt and append the team's own rules on top of it
Move the safety and tool-usage rules into CLAUDE.md, since CLAUDE.md replaces the minimal default prompt

questions.explanation: With no system prompt set, the Agent SDK uses a minimal prompt that covers tool calling but omits the Claude Code preset's content, including its security and safety instructions, while claude -p uses the Claude Code prompt by default. For a coding tool that a human watches and steers, the docs recommend the claude_code preset, with append for product-specific rules, as the lowest-risk customization. A custom string replaces the default entirely, so the team would have to rewrite the lost guidance itself. Setting sources and CLAUDE.md add project context to the conversation but do not change which system prompt is used.

questions.question: A startup wants Claude to run multi-hour autonomous tasks that execute shell commands, edit files, and browse the web. The team does not want to build or operate its own agent loop, sandbox, or tool execution layer, and it wants conversation history and sandbox state persisted server-side. Which option best fits?

options.text: Call the Messages API directly and implement a custom tool loop that runs commands on the team's own servers
Use the Message Batches API so long tasks can run for up to 24 hours without a persistent connection
Use the Claude Agent SDK, which runs the Claude Code agent inside a process the team operates
Use Claude Managed Agents, which provides a hosted agent harness with sessions in a managed sandbox

questions.explanation: Claude Managed Agents is a pre-built agent harness running on managed infrastructure, best for long-running and asynchronous work, with stateful sessions and built-in bash, file, and web tools. A custom Messages API loop and the Agent SDK both require the team to operate the runtime themselves. The Message Batches API processes independent Messages requests asynchronously and does not run tools in a sandbox for the team.

questions.question: A platform team wants to embed an agent in its existing Python service. The agent must read and edit files, run commands, and support hooks and permission controls, and it must run inside infrastructure the team already operates. Which option should the team choose?

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK, which provides Claude Code's agent loop, built-in tools, hooks, and permissions as a library
Claude Managed Agents, which runs every session in an Anthropic-hosted sandbox configured through the API
The Messages API with the Files API, which executes file edits and shell commands on the team's behalf
The token counting endpoint combined with Message Batches to schedule each agent step as a batch request

questions.explanation: The Agent SDK embeds Claude Code's agent loop, built-in tools, hooks, permissions, and sessions in Python or TypeScript applications running in a process you operate. Managed Agents is the option for having Anthropic host the agent harness. The Files API stores and references files but does not run commands or edit files. Token counting and batches do not provide an agent loop.

questions.question: A healthcare company operating entirely in AWS must meet HIPAA-ready compliance requirements and requires AWS to be the sole data processor for model inference. Which way of accessing Claude best meets these requirements?

options.text: Claude Platform on AWS, because Anthropic runs inference while AWS handles billing and IAM
The Claude API directly, using API keys stored in AWS Secrets Manager for authentication
Amazon Bedrock, because AWS operates the inference stack and acts as the data processor
Claude Managed Agents with a self-hosted sandbox deployed into the company's AWS account

questions.explanation: On Amazon Bedrock, AWS operates the inference stack and is the data processor, and the docs recommend Bedrock when you need HIPAA-ready or similar regulated compliance or need AWS as the sole data processor. On Claude Platform on AWS, Anthropic runs inference and is the data processor, and HIPAA readiness is listed as not supported. The direct Claude API and Managed Agents both involve Anthropic processing the data.

questions.question: A team has a working Python integration built on the Anthropic SDK and must move inference to Google Cloud's Agent Platform (Vertex AI) so usage runs under Google Cloud billing and IAM. They want to change as little application code as possible and not hand-maintain the platform's request-format differences. What should they do?

options.text: Keep the existing client and Anthropic API key, and point the client's base URL at the Google Cloud endpoint
Rewrite the calls as raw rawPredict HTTP requests so the platform-specific request body is under the team's control
Keep calling the Claude API directly and export usage logs to Google Cloud for billing reconciliation each month
Switch to the SDK's Vertex client with Google Cloud credentials and keep the same messages calls

questions.explanation: On Agent Platform the request format differs from the Claude API: the model goes in the endpoint URL and anthropic_version is sent in the body with a Vertex-specific value. Anthropic's SDKs support the platform (for example AnthropicVertex with a project and region using Google credentials), so the same messages.create calls work and the SDK handles those differences. An Anthropic API key and a changed base URL do not authenticate to Google Cloud or produce the required request shape. Raw rawPredict calls work but leave the team maintaining the format differences by hand, and calling the Claude API directly does not move inference or billing to Google Cloud.

questions.question: A team runs a Claude Agent SDK agent on shared CI build machines. It must follow the conventions in the repository's CLAUDE.md, but it must not pick up personal instructions or memory stored in the build account's home directory. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Leave the setting sources option unset, because by default the SDK loads only the repository's project settings
Set setting sources to project only, which loads the repository CLAUDE.md and leaves out user and local settings
Pass an empty setting sources list, which keeps the repository CLAUDE.md but drops everything from the home directory
Select the Claude Code preset system prompt, because CLAUDE.md is only loaded when that preset is in use
Disable auto memory through the agent's environment, since setting sources do not control it

questions.explanation: Setting sources to project only loads the repository's CLAUDE.md, rules, and settings while excluding the user source (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and user settings) and local files. Auto memory under ~/.claude/projects/ is read regardless of setting sources, so it must be turned off separately, for example with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1 in env. Omitting the option is equivalent to user, project, and local, so personal settings would load. An empty list disables the project source too, so the repository CLAUDE.md would not load, and CLAUDE.md loading is controlled by setting sources, not by the claude_code preset.

questions.question: A developer's chatbot sends only the user's newest message on each Messages API call. Users complain that Claude forgets what they said two turns earlier. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: The conversation ID header is missing; pass the previous response id so the API can reload the thread
The system prompt is too short; add an instruction telling Claude to remember earlier turns
The Messages API is stateless; resend the full conversation history in the messages array each call
Prompt caching is disabled; enable cache_control so the API stores earlier turns between calls

questions.explanation: The Messages API is stateless, so you always send the full conversational history to build a multi-turn conversation. There is no conversation-ID mechanism that reloads prior turns on the Messages API. A system prompt instruction cannot recall turns that were never sent, and prompt caching only reuses identical prefixes you send; it does not store conversation state for you.

questions.question: Users of a writing assistant see a blank screen for many seconds while Claude generates long answers, and they think the app has frozen. The developer wants text to appear as it is generated. What should the developer do?

options.text: Set stream to true (or use the SDK stream helper) and render each text_delta as it arrives over server-sent events
Lower max_tokens so each response finishes sooner, then request continuations until the answer is complete
Submit the request through the Message Batches API and poll every second for the partial result
Call the token counting endpoint first and display a progress bar based on the expected output length

questions.explanation: Setting stream to true returns the response incrementally as server-sent events, and content_block_delta events with text_delta deltas can be rendered as they arrive. Lowering max_tokens truncates answers and adds round trips. Batches are asynchronous and do not stream partial results. The token counting endpoint counts input tokens only, so it cannot predict output length.

questions.question: A team is building a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline on Claude and needs to embed 2 million document chunks for semantic search. How should they generate the embeddings?

options.text: Call the Messages API with an embeddings output format so Claude returns a vector for each chunk
Use the token counting endpoint, which returns per-token vectors that can be averaged into embeddings
Upload each chunk with the Files API, which automatically indexes files into a searchable vector store
Use a third-party embeddings provider such as Voyage AI, because Anthropic does not offer an embedding model

questions.explanation: Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model; the docs point to providers such as Voyage AI and suggest evaluating several vendors. The Messages API generates text, not embedding vectors. The token counting endpoint returns only an input token count, and the Files API stores files for reference in requests without building a vector index.

questions.question: A legal research tool must show users the exact passages from supplied contracts that support each statement Claude makes. The current prompt asks Claude to quote sources, but quotes are sometimes inaccurate and inflate output costs. What should the developer do?

options.text: Lower the temperature to zero and add a system prompt instruction to quote passages verbatim
Pass the contracts as document blocks with citations enabled and render the returned citation data
Request structured JSON output with a quotes array and validate each quote against the contract text
Upload the contracts with the Files API and ask Claude to include file offsets for every claim

questions.explanation: Enabling citations on document blocks makes the API return parsed citations with valid pointers into the provided documents, and the cited_text field does not count toward output tokens. Sampling and prompting changes do not guarantee accurate quotes. Structured outputs cannot be combined with citations and still relies on model-generated quotes. The Files API only supplies the document; citations still have to be enabled on the document block.

questions.question: A product team prototyped a support assistant in claude.ai, where Claude knew the current date and formatted code in Markdown. Their Messages API version, sent with no system parameter, does neither consistently. What explains the difference?

options.text: The API strips Markdown and date context unless the request sets an output_config format
The claude.ai system prompt published in the release notes does not apply to the Claude API
API models are trained separately from the claude.ai models and lack that behavior by default
claude.ai Project instructions sync to the API only when both use the same organization

questions.explanation: Anthropic's release notes explain that claude.ai and the mobile apps use a system prompt that supplies information such as the current date and encourages behaviors like Markdown code snippets, and that these system prompt updates do not apply to the Claude API. An API request with no system parameter gets none of that, so the developer must write their own system prompt with the context and formatting rules they need. output_config controls structured output, not date context. The difference comes from claude.ai's system prompt rather than a separately trained model, and claude.ai Project instructions are not carried into API calls.

questions.question: A developer on macOS has several MCP servers configured in the Claude Desktop app and wants the same servers available to Claude Code in every project without retyping each definition. What should the developer do?

options.text: Nothing, because Claude Code reads claude_desktop_config.json automatically at startup
Copy the whole claude_desktop_config.json file into the repository root as .mcp.json
Enable each Desktop server from the /mcp panel inside a Claude Code session in the project
Run claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop with --scope user and pick the servers to import

questions.explanation: Claude Code provides claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop, which reads the Claude Desktop configuration file from its standard location on macOS and WSL and lets you select servers to import; the --scope user flag adds them to the user configuration so they apply across projects. Claude Code does not pick up the Desktop config on its own, because the two apps keep separate MCP configuration. Copying the file into .mcp.json would create project-scoped, shared config rather than personal config for every project. The /mcp panel manages servers Claude Code already knows about; it does not import Desktop definitions.

questions.question: A due-diligence app sends Claude a user question plus about 40,000 tokens drawn from five supplier contracts, currently pasted as one block after the question. Answers sometimes attribute clauses to the wrong supplier. Which prompt structure follows Anthropic's guidance?

options.text: Place the contracts first, each in <document> tags with <source> and <document_content>, and the question last
Place the question first, then the contracts as one block, ending with a reminder to keep suppliers separate
Move the five contracts into the system prompt and send only the question in the user message on each call
Send each contract in its own API call and ask Claude to merge the five partial answers in a final request

questions.explanation: Anthropic's long-context guidance says to put longform data near the top of the prompt, above the query and instructions, and to wrap each of multiple documents in <document> tags with <document_content> and <source> metadata subtags for clarity. Labeling each contract's source is what lets Claude keep clauses attributed to the right supplier. Leaving the documents as one undifferentiated block keeps the ambiguity, and a reminder does not fix it. Moving the contracts into the system prompt still leaves them unlabeled by source, and splitting into separate calls prevents cross-document comparison and adds requests.

questions.question: An inspection app lets users attach several photos per turn in long multi-turn conversations. Images are sent as base64 every turn, and request size and latency grow steadily until some requests are rejected. What is the best design change?

options.text: Switch every image to a URL source hosted on a public bucket so the API caches them between turns
Drop all earlier images from the history and ask users to re-upload any photo they want to discuss again
Upload each image once with the Files API and reference it by file_id in every subsequent request
Convert all photos to a single animated GIF per turn so that only one image block is sent each time

questions.explanation: Because every request resends the full history, base64 images repeat their full bytes each turn; the vision docs recommend uploading to the Files API and referencing file_id to keep payloads small regardless of how many images accumulate. Public URLs raise exposure concerns and are not described as cached between turns. Dropping history loses context, and animated GIFs are unsupported beyond the first frame.

questions.question: A SaaS company builds a multi-tenant document Q&A product on the Files API. Each customer uploads private files, and the client app currently sends a file_id with each question. A security review flags a risk. What should the team do?

options.text: Rename each file with the tenant ID at upload so the API rejects cross-tenant file_id references
Keep file_id mapping server-side, never accept file IDs from clients, and use a workspace per tenant
Mark uploaded files as non-downloadable so other tenants cannot read them even with the file_id
Set a short expiration on every upload so leaked file IDs stop working before they can be misused

questions.explanation: Uploaded files are accessible to the entire workspace, so a user-supplied file_id could let one tenant read another's content; the docs say to treat file IDs as server-side references and use a separate workspace per tenant for isolation. Files cannot be renamed and filenames do not enforce access. Uploaded files are already non-downloadable but can still be used in Messages requests, and expiration only narrows the window.

questions.question: An email-triage agent returns each fetched email in a tool_result block, and the developer appends the line "Now classify this email as urgent or routine" inside that same tool_result text. Claude sometimes ignores the line or flags it as a possible injection. What should the developer change?

options.text: Repeat the classification instruction in capital letters inside the tool_result so it stands out
Move the fetched email body into the system prompt so it carries the same trust as the instruction
Send the classification instruction in a user turn that follows the tool_result block
Put the email and the instruction together in one plain user text block instead of a tool_result

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance says not to put your own instructions in tool results, because Claude treats tool-result content as untrusted data and may ignore or flag instructions there; instructions belong in a user turn that follows the tool_result block. Emphasis inside the tool result does not change how that content is trusted. Third-party content should be delivered only in tool_result blocks, never in the system prompt or plain user text blocks, so moving the email there would weaken the boundary between untrusted data and the developer's instructions. Merging both into one user text block erases the same boundary.

questions.question: A financial analyst tool extracts text from quarterly-report PDFs with a local library and sends only the text to Claude. Claude cannot answer questions about the charts and tables in the reports. What should the developer do?

options.text: Send the PDF itself as a document content block so Claude receives each page as both text and an image
Increase max_tokens so Claude has enough room to reconstruct the charts from the extracted text
Enable citations on the extracted text so Claude can reference the charts by their page numbers
Send the extracted text through the Message Batches API, which adds visual analysis of attachments

questions.explanation: With PDF support, each page is converted to an image and its text is extracted and provided alongside, so Claude can analyze charts, tables, and visual layouts. Raising max_tokens affects output length, not what Claude can see. Citations on plain text cannot recover visual content that was never sent, and batches process the same request content asynchronously without adding visual analysis.

questions.question: A team's production app sends a large, identical system prompt and tool list on every request and recently launched with a sudden traffic spike. It now receives frequent 429 rate_limit_error responses. Which TWO changes are most likely to reduce these errors? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Lower max_tokens on every request so less output capacity is reserved against the OTPM limit
Cache the shared system prompt and tools, since cache reads do not count toward ITPM on most models
Switch from the anthropic-ratelimit headers to a fixed one-request-per-second client throttle
Treat 429 responses as non-retryable and drop those requests to keep the queue moving
Ramp traffic up gradually and keep usage patterns consistent to avoid acceleration limits

questions.explanation: For most models only uncached input tokens count toward ITPM, so caching repeated system prompts and tools raises effective throughput, and sharp usage increases can trigger acceleration-limit 429s that are avoided by ramping gradually. max_tokens does not factor into OTPM calculations, so lowering it does not help. Ignoring the rate-limit headers and dropping retryable requests both make the app less resilient, not less limited.

questions.question: A loan app uses structured outputs so every response matches a JSON schema, and the business requires credit_score to be between 300 and 850 and notes to stay under 500 characters. Adding those bounds as schema keywords made every request fail with HTTP 400. How should the developer enforce the limits?

options.text: Keep the bounds only in the field descriptions and rely on structured outputs to enforce what the descriptions say
Drop the bounds from the sent schema and check them in application code after the response is parsed
Turn off structured outputs and request JSON in the prompt, since prompt instructions can express any limit
Move the bounds into the system prompt and lower the temperature so the model stays inside the ranges

questions.explanation: Structured outputs do not support numeric bounds such as minimum and maximum or string limits such as maxLength, and using them returns a 400 error. The SDK helpers handle this by removing unsupported constraints from the sent schema, noting them in the field description, and validating the response against the original schema (for example messages.parse with a Pydantic model), which amounts to enforcing the bounds in code. Descriptions are guidance to the model, not enforced constraints. Prompt-only JSON loses the schema guarantee, and prompt wording or sampling changes still cannot guarantee a value stays in range.

questions.question: A reporting service uses structured outputs, and a downstream parser reads the returned fields by position. After an optional notes field was added at the top of the schema, the parser broke because notes now appears after the required fields. The team wants a fix that keeps working as the schema evolves. What should they do?

options.text: Change the parser to read fields by key, because output order depends on which fields are required
Move notes to the bottom of the schema and add a comment telling future editors to keep optional fields last
Switch from structured outputs to requesting JSON in the prompt, which keeps fields in the order they are listed
Sort the returned keys alphabetically in a post-processing step before the parser reads them by position

questions.explanation: With structured outputs, required properties are emitted first and optional properties after them, each group in schema order, so adding an optional field can change positions. The docs say to mark all properties required or account for the reordering in parsing logic, and reading by key is the robust choice as the schema changes. Reordering the schema fixes today's case but breaks again the next time someone adds or makes a field optional. Dropping structured outputs gives up the schema guarantee, and alphabetical sorting still breaks positional parsing whenever a field is added.

questions.question: A developer spends an hour in one Claude Code session fixing a flaky integration test, then wants Claude to draft a database migration for an unrelated billing feature. Which step follows Claude Code's best practices before starting the migration?

options.text: Run /clear to start the migration in a fresh context, keeping CLAUDE.md project memory
Run /compact so the test-fixing details are summarized and carried into the migration work
Keep going in the same session so Claude can reuse what it learned about the codebase
Run /branch so the migration work continues from the current conversation in a branch

questions.explanation: Claude Code's best practices describe the kitchen sink session, where unrelated tasks share one context full of irrelevant information, and the fix is to run /clear between unrelated tasks. /clear starts a new conversation with empty context while project memory such as CLAUDE.md still loads. /compact keeps the same conversation and carries a summary of the test work forward, which is useful for continuing one task, not switching to an unrelated one. Staying in the same session or branching from it keeps the stale context that degrades performance.

questions.question: A developer runs two long-lived Claude Code workstreams in the same directory, an OAuth migration and a search rewrite, switching between them over several days. Each workstream needs its own context, and the developer wants to jump straight back into the right one without picking from a list. What should they do?

options.text: Always continue the most recent conversation in the directory and restate which workstream is active
Keep both workstreams in one session and compact the conversation whenever they switch between them
Give each session a descriptive name and resume it by that name when switching workstreams
Fork the current session each morning so that a fresh copy is created for whichever workstream is next

questions.explanation: Claude Code lets you set a display name for a session with --name (or change it with /rename) and resume a named session directly with claude --resume <name>, so each workstream keeps its own context and can be reopened without a picker. Continuing the most recent conversation picks whichever session was last used in the directory, which may be the wrong workstream. Mixing both tasks in one session pollutes context, and compaction only summarizes it. Forking creates a new session ID when resuming and does not give each workstream a stable, separate thread.

questions.question: A developer wants to try a third-party Claude Code plugin in one repository only, without it turning on for teammates who clone the repository and without it loading in their other projects. Which install scope should they choose?

options.text: User scope, which records the plugin in ~/.claude/settings.json for every project
Local scope, which records the plugin in .claude/settings.local.json for this repository only
Project scope, which records the plugin in the committed .claude/settings.json for the repository
Managed scope, which records the plugin in managed-settings.json for this machine

questions.explanation: Local scope enables the plugin for you in this repository only, and the entry goes in .claude/settings.local.json, which is not shared with collaborators. User scope writes to ~/.claude/settings.json and enables the plugin in every project on the machine. Project scope writes to the committed .claude/settings.json and turns the plugin on for everyone who works in the repository. Managed settings are an organization policy mechanism, not a personal install scope, and they apply across the machine.

questions.question: An application's error handler only catches exceptions raised by the SDK. Occasionally users see an empty or partial answer, and logs show HTTP 200 responses with stop_reason "refusal". How should the developer handle this case?

options.text: Catch the SDK's PermissionDeniedError, which is raised whenever Claude declines to respond
Retry the same request unchanged, since refusals are transient overload conditions on the server
Treat it as a max_tokens truncation and resend the request with a larger output budget
Check stop_reason on successful responses, read stop_details, and consider a fallback model

questions.explanation: A refusal arrives as a normal HTTP 200 response with stop_reason "refusal" rather than as an error, so code must inspect stop_reason, read stop_details for the policy category, and consider retrying on a fallback model. No exception is raised for refusals, they are not overload conditions, and they are unrelated to the max_tokens limit.

questions.question: A developer streams Messages API responses so text appears as it is generated, and also needs the final stop reason and output token count for billing. Their hand-written SSE parser reads usage from the first event of each stream and records far too few output tokens. What is the best fix?

options.text: Use the SDK's stream helper and read stop reason and usage from its final accumulated message
Call the token counting endpoint after each stream ends and bill on the count it returns for the response
Disable streaming for billing-relevant calls so the usage block is always complete in a single response
Count the text deltas received during the stream and multiply by an average tokens-per-delta factor

questions.explanation: The first streaming event arrives before any output is generated, while the stop reason and cumulative usage counts come in the message_delta events near the end of the stream. The SDKs' streaming helpers accumulate every event into the complete Message (for example get_final_message in Python or finalMessage in TypeScript), so the app can render text live and still read accurate final values. The token counting endpoint returns only the input tokens of a request, not what a response generated. Turning off streaming breaks the live-text requirement, and estimating from delta counts is inaccurate.

questions.question: A platform team must make sure every developer in the company gets an internal code-formatter plugin from the company's GitHub-hosted marketplace, and individual developers must not be able to switch it off. How should the team configure this?

options.text: Commit enabledPlugins for the plugin to each repository's .claude/settings.json and ask developers to accept trust
Ask each developer to run /plugin marketplace add for the company repo and install the plugin at user scope
Publish the plugin to Anthropic's official marketplace so it is added automatically for every user
Set extraKnownMarketplaces and enabledPlugins in managed settings so every machine installs and enables it

questions.explanation: In managed settings, extraKnownMarketplaces registers the marketplace on each machine and enabledPlugins names the plugins to install and enable from it; Claude Code installs them at the user's next session, and disabling one at a user's own scope does not stop it because managed settings take precedence over every other scope. Repository .claude/settings.json covers only that repository's contributors, applies the marketplace only after folder trust, and can be overridden by local settings. Asking developers to install manually does not guarantee coverage or prevent disabling. Publishing to Anthropic's official marketplace does not install or enable a plugin for anyone.

questions.question: During peak hours, a streaming chat feature sometimes stops mid-answer even though the HTTP response status was 200. The developer's HTTP-status-based error handling never triggers. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The client is ignoring ping events, which causes the server to close the stream
The API returned a 413 status for the long answer, but the SDK masked it as a 200
An error event such as overloaded_error was sent inside the stream after the 200
The stream reached max_tokens, which the API reports by sending a 529 status

questions.explanation: With SSE streaming, errors can occur after the API has returned a 200, arriving as an error event (for example overloaded_error, which corresponds to HTTP 529 in non-streaming calls), so standard status-code handling does not catch them. Ping events can be ignored safely. A 413 is returned before processing and is not masked, and max_tokens is reported through stop_reason, not an error status.

questions.question: A developer has several Claude Code plugins installed at user scope but uses most of them only in occasional sessions, and every session now starts with less free context. They want to reclaim that context without losing the ability to turn the plugins back on quickly. Which TWO actions best meet this goal? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Disable the occasional plugins with /plugin or claude plugin disable, which leaves them installed
Uninstall the occasional plugins and reinstall each one from its marketplace whenever it is needed again
Leave them enabled, because a plugin adds nothing to context until one of its skills is actually invoked
Use the plugin manager's list of plugins not used recently to decide which ones to turn off
Run occasional work in the desktop app instead, since it does not load plugins installed from the terminal

questions.explanation: An enabled plugin is part of every session: the name and description of each skill, agent, and command Claude can invoke are in context on every turn, even when nothing from the plugin runs. Disabling a plugin with /plugin or claude plugin disable stops that cost without uninstalling it, and the Installed tab's Not used recently group shows which plugins are candidates to turn off. Uninstalling also frees context but fails the requirement to turn plugins back on quickly. Plugins are not free until invoked, and the terminal and the desktop app's local sessions read the same settings files, so switching surfaces does not help.

questions.question: A team runs a support agent on Claude Managed Agents and has rewritten the agent's system prompt. They want production sessions to keep using the current prompt while staging sessions exercise the new one, then promote it on their own schedule. What should the developer do?

options.text: Start every production session by passing the agent ID as a plain string, which keeps the version in use when the session was first set up
Send the old version number in the agent update request, so sessions keep using that version until a later update supplies a new one
Update the agent, which creates a new version, and pin production sessions to the old version with an agent object that sets version
Copy the new system prompt into each staging session's first user message, since agent updates overwrite the stored prompt in place

questions.explanation: A Managed Agents agent is a versioned resource: an update that changes the configuration creates a new version, and a session can be pinned to a specific version by passing an agent object with type, id, and version, which lets teams stage rollouts independently. Passing the agent ID as a string does the opposite of what option A claims; it creates the session with the latest version. The version field in an update request is for optimistic concurrency (a mismatch returns 409), not for choosing which version sessions run. Updates do not overwrite earlier versions, so pasting the prompt into user messages is unnecessary and bypasses the versioned configuration.

questions.question: A team's committed .claude/settings.json sets the model to a Sonnet model. One developer wants Claude Code to use an Opus model in this repository only, for their own sessions, without changing what teammates get or adding a commit. Where should the developer set it?

options.text: In .claude/settings.local.json in the project, which applies over the shared project file
In ~/.claude/settings.json, since user settings apply over any project's shared settings
In .claude/settings.json, after asking teammates to override it back in their own files
In managed-settings.json on their machine, since only managed values beat a project file

questions.explanation: Claude Code's settings precedence, highest first, is managed settings, command line (--settings), project local (.claude/settings.local.json), shared project (.claude/settings.json), and then user (~/.claude/settings.json). A model set in .claude/settings.local.json therefore overrides the committed team value for that developer only, and Claude Code keeps that file out of git when it creates it. User settings sit below shared project settings, so ~/.claude/settings.json would lose to the team's file. Editing the shared file changes everyone's sessions and requires a commit, and managed settings are an organization-deployed policy tier, not a personal override mechanism.

questions.question: A team is building a weekly re-scoring pipeline that submits thousands of classification requests through the Message Batches API and writes each result back to the matching database row. Which TWO design choices matter most for correctness? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Match each result to its row by position, since results come back in the order the requests were submitted
Set stream to true on each batched request so rows can be updated as soon as each answer is generated
Give every request a unique custom_id derived from the row key, and match results using that ID
Count on batch creation to reject any malformed request immediately, so the pipeline fails fast
Send one sample request through the regular Messages API first to confirm the request shape is valid

questions.explanation: Batch results can be returned in any order, so each request needs a unique custom_id that the pipeline uses to match results to rows. Params are validated asynchronously and validation errors come back only when the whole batch has ended, so the docs recommend checking the request shape with the Messages API first. Matching by position fails because order is not guaranteed. Streaming is not supported inside batch requests, since results come back as a file, and batch creation does not fail fast on malformed params.

questions.question: A team must call the Messages API over raw HTTP from a language that has no official SDK. They want the integration to keep working as Anthropic evolves the API, and to adopt changes only when they choose. What should they do?

options.text: Send an explicit API version header and ignore unknown response fields and new enum values
Omit the version header so the API always serves its newest behavior and the client never falls behind
Send the newest beta headers on every request so the client receives new features before they are stable
Validate responses against a strict schema that rejects any field or value the client was not written for

questions.explanation: Every request must send an anthropic-version header (the SDKs set it automatically), and within a version Anthropic preserves existing input and output parameters. Anthropic may still add optional inputs, add values to the output, and add new variants to enum-like values such as streaming event types, so a raw client should tolerate unknown fields and values. Omitting the header is not an option, because the header is required. Beta headers opt into pre-release features rather than stability, and a strict validator would break on the additive changes that a version allows.

questions.question: During a high-traffic period, an application using the official Python SDK logs occasional 529 overloaded_error responses. The team wants transient failures handled with backoff but wants more attempts than the default. What should they do?

options.text: Rely on the SDK's built-in exponential-backoff retries and raise max_retries on the client
Treat 529 as a billing problem and check payment details in the Console before retrying
Write a loop that retries immediately without delay, since the SDK never retries 5xx errors
Switch all traffic to the token counting endpoint until the overload clears and then resume

questions.explanation: 529 overloaded_error means the API is temporarily overloaded. The official SDKs automatically retry transient failures, including rate limits and 5xx errors, with exponential backoff (twice by default, honoring retry-after), and max_retries configures this. Billing issues return 402, not 529. Immediate retries without delay worsen overload, and the token counting endpoint does not generate responses.

questions.question: A platform team's deploy-kit plugin calls an MCP tool provided by a secrets-vault plugin in the same git-backed marketplace, and a secrets-vault 2.2 release renamed that tool and broke deploy-kit for users who updated. The team wants users to keep getting 2.1.x fixes and move to 2.2 only after the team has tested it. What should they do?

options.text: Declare secrets-vault as a dependency with a ~2.1.0 range, and make sure its releases are tagged
Copy secrets-vault's MCP server into deploy-kit so that deploy-kit no longer relies on the separate plugin
Pin deploy-kit's own version number to 2.1.0 so that the plugins it relies on stay on the same release line
Ask every user to turn off marketplace auto-update and update secrets-vault by hand after each test round

questions.explanation: A plugin can list other plugins as dependencies in its plugin.json with a semantic-version range, and a constraint such as ~2.1.0 keeps users on 2.1.x patches without moving to 2.2; the team widens the range after testing a newer release. For git-backed sources the range resolves against release tags, so the dependency's releases must be tagged. Vendoring the MCP server cuts users off from secrets-vault's 2.1.x fixes. deploy-kit's own version field does not constrain its dependencies, and relying on every user to change update settings is not enforceable.

questions.question: An organization on a Claude Enterprise plan with Zero Data Retention enabled wants Claude to review every pull request in its GitHub repositories automatically and post findings as PR comments. Which approach fits these constraints?

options.text: Have an Owner turn on the managed Code Review service, which reviews PR activity on Anthropic infrastructure for Enterprise organizations
Add a Claude Code GitHub Actions workflow on pull_request events that runs a review skill with --comment on the team's own runners
Install the Claude GitHub App and rely on reviewers typing an @claude mention on each pull request to trigger the interactive mode
Ask each developer to run /code-review on their branch in a local Claude Code session before they open each pull request on GitHub

questions.explanation: The managed Code Review service is not available to organizations with Zero Data Retention enabled, so option A is ruled out by the stated constraint. Claude in your own CI with GitHub Actions runs on your own runners, and a workflow triggered on pull_request events with a review skill and the --comment argument posts the review on every pull request automatically. Interactive mode waits for someone to type @claude, so it does not review every PR without human action. Local /code-review depends on each developer remembering to run it and does not provide automatic coverage of every pull request.

questions.question: A nightly summarization job calls the Claude API directly over HTTP (no SDK). During peak hours some requests fail with HTTP 529 overloaded_error, and the job aborts. What should the developer do?

options.text: Retry failed requests immediately in a tight loop until each one succeeds, since 529 errors clear within milliseconds.
Treat 529 as a permanent failure, skip the request, and lower max_tokens on every later request to reduce load.
Retry transient errors such as 529, 429, and 500 with exponential backoff, honoring the retry-after header when present.
Retry every non-2xx response, including 400 and 401 errors, with the same fixed delay between attempts.

questions.explanation: A 529 means the API is temporarily overloaded, so it is a transient error. The right handling is to retry with exponential backoff and honor retry-after when it is sent, which is also how the official SDKs retry. Tight-loop retries add load and keep failing. Treating 529 as permanent throws away work that would succeed later. Retrying 400 or 401 is pointless, because a malformed request or a bad key fails the same way every time.

questions.question: A production service suddenly gets HTTP 429 rate_limit_error on every request. The response has no retry-after header, and error.details.error_code is enforced_spend_limit_reached. The SDK's automatic retries keep failing. What is the most likely cause, and what should the team do?

options.text: The organization reached its usage tier's monthly spend cap, so retries will fail until access resumes; alert operators and request a higher tier.
A per-minute token limit was exceeded, so the team should raise max_retries until the token bucket refills and requests succeed again.
The API is overloaded across all users, so the team should wait a few seconds and resend the same requests with jittered backoff.
The API key expired, so the team should rotate the key in the secrets manager and redeploy the service with the new key.

questions.explanation: A tier spend-cap 429 has no retry-after header, sets error_code to enforced_spend_limit_reached, and keeps failing until access resumes, so retries cannot help. Moving to a higher tier restores access. A per-minute rate limit 429 usually clears with backoff, but this response is the spend cap, not a per-minute limit. Overload is a 529 error, not a 429, and an expired key returns 401 authentication_error.

questions.question: A developer wants two Claude Code sessions running at the same time on one repository: one building a new auth feature and one fixing an unrelated bug. In a quick trial both sessions edited the same checkout and overwrote each other's changes. What should the developer do?

options.text: Run both sessions in the same checkout but put each task's file paths into CLAUDE.md so that each session stays within its own set of files
Clone the repository twice from the remote, since git worktrees share one working directory and would not keep the sessions' edits apart
Start each with claude --worktree and a distinct name, giving each session its own working directory and branch over shared history
Run the bug fix as a subagent in the feature session, because subagents always edit a separate copy of the files from the main session

questions.explanation: A git worktree is a separate working directory with its own files and branch that shares the repository's history and remote, and claude --worktree <name> starts a session inside one so parallel sessions' edits do not collide. Running the command again with a different name in another terminal starts a second isolated session. CLAUDE.md instructions guide behavior but do not isolate files on disk. Worktrees do not share a working directory, so a second full clone is unnecessary, and a subagent does not get a separate copy of the files unless it is explicitly given worktree isolation.

questions.question: A Python service shares one Anthropic client between a nightly document-analysis job and an inline autocomplete feature. Autocomplete must fall back to a cached suggestion if Claude has not answered within 5 seconds. The nightly job must keep its long default timeout. How should the developer configure this?

options.text: Set timeout=5.0 when constructing the shared client so every request, including the nightly job, fails fast together.
Keep the client defaults and call client.with_options(timeout=5.0) for the autocomplete requests only.
Set max_tokens to a small value on the autocomplete requests, because max_tokens acts as a wall-clock limit.
Set the ANTHROPIC_LOG environment variable to info so the SDK cancels slow requests after five seconds.

questions.explanation: The SDK takes a timeout at the client level and lets you override it per request with with_options(), so only autocomplete calls get the 5-second limit. A client-wide 5-second timeout would break the long nightly job. max_tokens caps output length, not elapsed time. ANTHROPIC_LOG controls logging verbosity and has no effect on timeouts.

questions.question: An on-call engineer needs to escalate a handful of failed and slow Claude API calls to Anthropic support. The application logs only the prompt text and a timestamp. What should the team add to its logging so these issues can be investigated quickly?

options.text: The request-id response header value, exposed as _request_id on SDK response objects and request_id in error bodies.
The full API key used for each request, so support can look up the matching account and its history.
The anthropic-version header value sent on each call, since support uses the version value to locate individual requests.
A locally generated UUID per call, which Anthropic support can match against its server logs without any other identifiers.

questions.explanation: Every API response carries a unique request-id header, which the Python and TypeScript SDKs expose as _request_id and which also appears as request_id in error bodies. Including it when you contact support helps them resolve issues quickly. Never log a full API key. anthropic-version is the same on almost every request, so it can't identify one call. A locally generated UUID never reaches Anthropic's servers.

questions.question: A team's asyncio-based web service calls the synchronous Anthropic Python client inside its async request handlers. Under load, each slow Claude call blocks other unrelated requests from being served. Which change best addresses this?

options.text: Increase max_retries on the synchronous client so that each blocked request eventually completes and frees the event loop sooner.
Create a new synchronous Anthropic client for every incoming request so that each client has its own separate connection.
Use the AsyncAnthropic client and await its calls, bounding concurrency with a semaphore to stay within rate limits.
Switch every call to the Message Batches API so the async handlers return immediately without waiting for any results.

questions.explanation: The SDK ships an AsyncAnthropic client with the same interface as the sync client. Awaiting it lets the event loop serve other requests while Claude responds, and a semaphore keeps the number of concurrent calls within rate limits. Retries don't stop the sync client from blocking the loop. A fresh sync client per request still blocks the loop. Batches are asynchronous jobs that can take up to 24 hours, which doesn't work for interactive handlers.

questions.question: A scheduler fires all of its Claude requests in a burst at the start of each minute. The total per minute is below the organization's RPM limit, but many requests in each burst get 429 errors. What should the developer do?

options.text: Wait for the fixed one-minute window to reset after each 429, then resend the whole burst at the start of the next minute.
Generate a second API key in the same organization and alternate the keys so that each burst draws on separate limits.
Raise max_tokens on every request so that fewer total requests are needed and the per-minute request count drops.
Spread requests evenly over time with a client-side throttle, because limits can be enforced over intervals shorter than a minute.

questions.explanation: Limits can be enforced over intervals shorter than a minute (for example, 60 RPM as 1 request per second), and the token bucket algorithm refills capacity continuously, so bursts can trigger 429s even when the per-minute total is under the limit. Smoothing traffic is the fix. Limits don't reset on fixed windows. Rate limits apply at the organization level, so a second key in the same organization adds no capacity. max_tokens doesn't reduce the number of requests the scheduler sends.

questions.question: A company switches a new Claude-powered feature on for its entire user base at once. Traffic jumps from almost nothing to a large volume within minutes, and the organization sees 429 errors even though usage is below its tier's published limits. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The model's context window filled up across concurrent users, which the API reports as a 429 until sessions are closed.
Acceleration limits on the API, triggered by the sharp increase in usage; ramping traffic up gradually avoids them.
The anthropic-version header is out of date, and the API throttles older versions more aggressively during spikes.
A workspace spend limit was reached, which always returns a 429 with a retry-after header for every workspace.

questions.explanation: A sharp increase in usage can trigger 429s from acceleration limits even below the tier limits. Anthropic recommends ramping traffic up gradually and keeping usage patterns consistent, for example with a staged rollout. A full context window returns a validation error, not a 429. There is no version-based throttling. A spend limit you set yourself returns a 400 invalid_request_error, except on the Claude Code workspace.

questions.question: An audit script calls client.messages.batches.list(limit=20) in the Python SDK and reads only the data field of the result. The script reports far fewer batches than the organization has created. What should the developer change?

options.text: Iterate over the returned list object with a for loop, which auto-paginates to fetch later pages as needed.
Remove the limit argument so the endpoint returns every batch ever created in one response.
Call the same list method repeatedly with the same arguments, because each call returns a different random page.
Switch to the Usage and Cost API, which is the only endpoint that can enumerate all of an organization's batches.

questions.explanation: List endpoints are paginated, so data holds only the current page and limit sets the page size. Iterating over the list result with for (or async for) fetches more pages automatically, and has_next_page() and get_next_page() are available for manual control. Removing limit still returns one page. Repeating a call with the same arguments doesn't page forward. The Usage and Cost API reports usage, not the batch objects themselves.

questions.question: An invoice-processing service on a current Claude model asks for JSON in the prompt and runs json.loads on the reply. It fails intermittently on malformed or missing fields. The team wants reliable typed parsing. What is the best approach?

options.text: Extract the first curly-brace block with a regular expression, and resend the prompt whenever the extracted block fails to parse.
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening curly brace so that the model is forced to continue with valid JSON output.
Use structured outputs with a JSON schema, for example messages.parse with a Pydantic model, and still check for max_tokens or refusal stops.
Ask the model to double-check its JSON in the system prompt and wrap json.loads in a retry loop with no upper bound.

questions.explanation: Structured outputs (output_config.format with a JSON schema, or the SDK's parse() helpers) constrain decoding so the response matches the schema. The output can still be incomplete when stop_reason is max_tokens, or off-schema when it is refusal, so those cases still need handling. Regex extraction is brittle. Claude 4.6 and later models reject assistant prefill with a 400 error. Unbounded retries waste cost and can loop forever.

questions.question: A team's CI unit tests call the live Claude API and assert exact output strings. The tests are slow, cost money, and fail randomly when wording varies. They want fast, deterministic unit tests for their integration code, and they still want to measure model quality. What should they do?

options.text: Keep calling the live API but set temperature to 0 on every request so that the output strings become exactly reproducible.
Raise max_retries in CI so that flaky failures are retried until the model happens to return the expected exact string.
Move the exact-string assertions to run against production traffic, so the assertions are checked on real user requests.
Point the SDK at a local stub server with base_url in unit tests, and measure model quality in a separate eval suite.

questions.explanation: The SDK accepts a base_url (or the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL environment variable), so unit tests can run against a stub that returns fixed responses and stay deterministic, fast, and free. Model quality belongs in evals with automated grading over many examples. API version 2026-10-21, which current SDKs send by default, removes temperature, so a request that sets it returns a 400 error on every model, and even on older versions where temperature 0 is accepted, outputs are not fully deterministic. Retrying until a match appears hides real failures. Asserting against production traffic is not a unit test.

questions.question: A service sets timeout=60 on its Python Anthropic client and makes non-streaming calls that produce long outputs. Logs show each logical call sent three times, each attempt cut off after about 60 seconds, and no response ever received. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The API returned 529 overloaded errors three times in a row, and the client reported them as timeouts in the logs.
Generation takes longer than the 60-second timeout, so the SDK drops each attempt and retries, twice by default.
The organization's output-token rate limit is being counted against max_tokens, so each attempt is throttled after 60 seconds.
The anthropic-version header is missing, so the API holds the connection open until the client gives up on each attempt.

questions.explanation: When a non-streaming request takes longer than the configured timeout, the client closes the connection and retries without receiving a response, and timed-out requests are retried twice by default. That produces three abandoned attempts. The fix is to stream or raise the timeout. A 529 returns an error response, not a silent cutoff. OTPM counts actual output tokens, not max_tokens. The SDK always sends anthropic-version.

questions.question: A developer's error handler checks whether the exception message contains the text "rate limit" and retries if it does, otherwise it fails the job. A code reviewer flags this as fragile. Which approach should the developer use?

options.text: Catch the SDK's typed exceptions, such as RateLimitError and APIConnectionError, handling the most specific first.
Search the message for a longer list of phrases such as overloaded and timeout, and keep adding phrases as new ones appear.
Treat every exception from the SDK as retryable, including validation and authentication errors, to keep the handler simple.
Disable the SDK's exceptions and inspect the raw HTTP body for keywords before deciding to retry.

questions.explanation: The SDK raises typed exceptions (for example RateLimitError for 429 and APIConnectionError for network failures). The docs advise catching these classes, most specific first, instead of string-matching messages, which can change. Growing the phrase list keeps the same fragility. Retrying 400 and 401 errors can never succeed. Parsing raw bodies for keywords is just string-matching again.

questions.question: A team is moving a Claude-powered service from a developer laptop to CI and production. Which TWO practices should they adopt for handling Claude API credentials? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Commit a .env file with the key to the private repository, so every environment and pipeline run picks up the same value.
Store the key in a secrets manager and inject it at runtime through the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable.
Reuse the lead developer's personal API key in CI and production, so every request is attributed to one known user.
Hardcode the key in a configuration file in base64-encoded form, so it isn't readable in plain text by reviewers.
Use a service account key for the shared workload, set an expiration, and rotate it or disable it if it may have leaked.

questions.explanation: Anthropic recommends storing keys in a secrets manager, rotating them, and disabling any key that may have leaked. The SDKs read ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment automatically. Shared or automated workloads should use a service account key, because a shared personal key acts as one person and stops working when that person leaves. Committing keys to a repository or hardcoding them, even base64-encoded, exposes the secret.

questions.question: A front-end developer wants a single-page web app to call Claude directly from the browser with the TypeScript SDK. The SDK refuses to run in the browser unless dangerouslyAllowBrowser is set to true. The app is public. What should the developer do?

options.text: Set dangerouslyAllowBrowser to true and minify the bundle so that the API key embedded in it is hard to find.
Set dangerouslyAllowBrowser to true and store the key in the browser's localStorage after the user first loads the page.
Keep the key on a backend service and have the browser call that backend, which makes the Claude API request.
Switch to the Python SDK in the browser through WebAssembly, which does not have the same browser restriction.

questions.explanation: The TypeScript SDK disables browser use by default, because shipping the key to the browser exposes it to anyone who inspects the page. A public app should keep the key server-side behind a backend. Minifying or using localStorage still sends the key to the client. Running a different SDK in the browser has the same exposure problem.

questions.question: An organization runs development, staging, and production traffic for the same Claude app. It wants to stop runaway test scripts from consuming production's capacity and to see costs per environment, while keeping centralized billing. What should it do?

options.text: Use one shared API key for all environments and tag each request with an environment label in the prompt text.
Create a separate organization for each environment, each with its own billing account and its own set of members.
Put development traffic in the Default Workspace and set lower rate and spend limits on that Default Workspace.
Create a workspace per environment with workspace-scoped keys, and give development lower rate and spend limits.

questions.explanation: Workspaces separate projects, environments, or teams within one organization, so billing stays centralized. Each workspace can have its own keys and custom rate and spend limits, and usage and cost can be tracked per workspace. A shared key with prompt labels gives no isolation or cost breakdown. Separate organizations break centralized billing. You can't set limits on the Default Workspace.

questions.question: A developer switches a service to a new service account API key that has access to several workspaces. Every request now fails with a 400 invalid_request_error saying anthropic-workspace-id is required. What should the developer do?

options.text: Send the anthropic-workspace-id header on every request, e.g. via the client's default headers.
Rotate the key, because a 400 error with this message means the new key has already expired.
Add an anthropic-version header, because multi-workspace keys require a newer API version.
Retry the requests with exponential backoff, because the new workspace is still being provisioned.

questions.explanation: A key that isn't scoped to a single workspace must name the target workspace in the anthropic-workspace-id header on every request, and it can be set once with the client's default headers. The alternative is a key scoped to one workspace. An expired key returns 401, not 400. The version header is unrelated to workspace selection. Retrying sends the same invalid request again.

questions.question: A regulated team uses a Claude model from before the 4.6 generation, referenced on the Claude API by its short alias. Their policy says the model behind production must never change without a code review. What should they do?

options.text: Keep the short alias, because the Claude API guarantees an alias always resolves to the snapshot it first pointed to.
Reference the full dated snapshot ID, because the alias points to the most recent snapshot for that minor version.
Pin the anthropic-version header to a fixed date, because that header also freezes which model snapshot serves requests.
Pin the SDK package version in the lockfile, because each SDK release hardcodes the snapshot behind every alias.

questions.explanation: For pre-4.6 models, an alias such as claude-sonnet-4-5 is a convenience pointer to the most recent dated snapshot for that minor version, so only the dated ID is fixed. From the 4.6 generation on, dateless IDs are themselves pinned snapshots. An alias carries no stability guarantee. anthropic-version governs API behavior, not model selection. SDK versions don't control alias resolution.

questions.question: A team has used the same dateless 4.6-generation-or-later model ID for months. Their monitoring flags small differences in observable behavior on a stable eval set, with no code, prompt, or model ID changes. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Anthropic silently retrained and updated the weights behind the existing model ID to improve its overall quality.
The dateless ID is an evergreen alias that was automatically moved to point at a newer model release.
An update to the serving infrastructure, such as routing, safety classifiers, or sampling logic, changed behavior slightly.
The SDK upgraded the anthropic-version header automatically, which changed how the model interprets every prompt.

questions.explanation: Weights are fixed for a given model ID, but the serving infrastructure around the model (request router, safety classifiers, sampling logic) can change. When behavior shifts on a stable ID, an infrastructure update is the most likely cause. Anthropic does not update weights under an existing ID. Dateless IDs from the 4.6 generation on are pinned snapshots, not evergreen aliases. The SDK sends a fixed anthropic-version value.

questions.question: A team wrote a custom HTTP client for the Messages API with a strict deserializer that rejects any unknown field or enum value. After a routine platform update, the parser starts throwing on responses that contain a new enum value. What should the team change?

options.text: Downgrade the anthropic-version header to 2023-01-01, which never adds new output values to responses.
Stop sending the anthropic-version header so the API falls back to a frozen legacy response format.
Report a breaking change, since the versioning policy forbids any new values in existing responses.
Make the parser tolerate unknown fields and new enum variants, since a version can add output values.

questions.explanation: For a given anthropic-version, Anthropic keeps existing input and output parameters but may add optional inputs, add output values, and add new variants to enum-like outputs such as streaming event types. Clients should be forward-compatible. Older versions are deprecated and may be unavailable. The header is required on raw HTTP requests. Adding output values is allowed under the policy, so it isn't a breaking change.

questions.question: A team wants to ship a beta API feature in a production service that also has a working GA code path. They want to limit the impact if the beta later changes and avoid surprises in cost or capacity. Which TWO practices best meet these goals? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Size capacity and budget from the GA feature's limits and prices, since a beta inherits both.
Turn the beta on only where needed, behind a switch that falls back to the GA code path.
Leave the beta name in the header after the beta ends, since unknown names are simply ignored.
Put the beta name in the API version header so the feature stays pinned to that dated version.
Follow release notes for the beta and retest before relying on changes, since betas can change.

questions.explanation: Beta features are experimental: they may have breaking changes with notice, be deprecated or removed, have different rate limits or pricing, and not be available in all regions, so gating the beta behind a fallback and tracking release notes contain that risk. Planning from GA limits and prices is wrong because betas can differ on both. An invalid or unavailable beta name returns a 400 error, so a stale beta name breaks requests rather than being ignored. Betas are requested with their own anthropic-beta header, separate from anthropic-version.

questions.question: A team wants Claude Code to migrate a large src/ tree from JavaScript to TypeScript. They want the change split into independent pieces that run in parallel, a plan they can approve first, and each piece tested and published separately. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Run /batch with the migration instruction, which plans units of work and runs each in its own worktree
Run /code-review --fix on the whole repository, so Claude rewrites each JavaScript file as a finding
Start one interactive session with plan mode off and ask Claude to convert every file in a single pass
Run /simplify on src/, which converts the files and removes leftover JavaScript once the build passes

questions.explanation: The bundled /batch skill orchestrates large-scale changes: it researches the codebase, decomposes the work into 5 to 30 independent units, presents a plan, and after approval spawns one background subagent per unit in an isolated worktree that implements, tests, and publishes its change. /code-review --fix applies review findings for correctness bugs, not a planned language migration. A single sequential session gives no parallelism or per-unit isolation. /simplify is a cleanup review for reuse and simplification, not a tool for decomposing and migrating a codebase.

questions.question: A legal-tech company has a Zero Data Retention arrangement for the Claude API. A business requirement says customer contract text must not be stored at rest by Anthropic, and the design must also reuse a large shared instruction block cheaply across requests. Which architecture meets the requirement?

options.text: Upload each contract once through the Files API and reference it by file_id in later Messages API requests
Queue the contracts into Message Batches API jobs overnight and use the batch discount to offset cost
Run each contract through the code execution tool so parsing happens in a container rather than in the prompt
Send contract text inline in standard Messages API calls and use prompt caching for the shared prefix

questions.explanation: Standard Messages API calls and prompt caching are both ZDR-eligible; for caching, prompts and outputs are not stored, and only KV cache representations are held in memory for the cache TTL. The Files API retains files until deletion or expiration, batch processing has 29-day retention, and code execution retains container data for up to 30 days, so none of those are ZDR-eligible. Under ZDR the API does not block non-eligible features, so using them would silently step outside the arrangement and violate the requirement. The requirement therefore has to be met by choosing eligible features in the architecture itself.

questions.question: A product manager asks for a Claude-based ticket classifier that is "accurate, fast, and not too expensive." Before building, the developer wants requirements that an eval can check. Which restatement is best?

options.text: At least 0.85 F1 on a held-out labeled set of real tickets, 95% of responses under a set latency, and a cost ceiling per 1,000 tickets.
Use the most capable model available with a detailed prompt, so accuracy, speed, and cost will all be acceptable by default.
Classifications should seem correct to the support team, responses should feel quick, and the monthly bill should look reasonable.
Achieve 100% accuracy on every possible ticket with zero latency, so no human review is needed once the classifier ships.

questions.explanation: Good success criteria are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant. Most applications need several dimensions, such as task fidelity, latency, and price, each with a concrete target. Defaulting to the most capable model sets no criteria at all. Option C is still subjective and can't be measured. Perfect accuracy with zero latency is not achievable.

questions.question: A customer-support chat assistant already gives good answers, but users complain that they stare at a blank screen until the full reply appears. The requirement is to make the assistant feel responsive without lowering answer quality. Which approach best meets this requirement?

options.text: Move the chat traffic to the Message Batches API so that responses are processed more efficiently in the background.
Raise max_tokens substantially so the model has more room to plan its reply and finishes generating it sooner.
Add more instructions and examples to the prompt so that the model has to spend less time deciding what to say.
Stream responses so text appears as it is generated, track time to first token, and trim unneeded prompt tokens.

questions.explanation: Streaming lets users see output as it is generated, which greatly improves perceived responsiveness. Time to first token is the metric to watch, and fewer input and output tokens also reduce latency. Batches are asynchronous and much slower to return. A higher max_tokens doesn't speed up generation. Adding prompt tokens tends to increase latency, not reduce it.

questions.question: A team needs to route millions of short inbound messages a day into one of a dozen queues. The requirements emphasize tight latency and low cost, and the task is fairly straightforward. Which model-selection approach aligns with Anthropic's guidance?

options.text: Start with the most capable model and keep it permanently, because classification quality always outweighs latency and cost.
Start with the fastest, lowest-cost tier such as Haiku, test thoroughly against evals, and upgrade only for real capability gaps.
Pick the model with the largest context window, because longer context always produces more accurate routing decisions.
Choose a model based on its public benchmark ranking alone, without building any evaluation set for this routing task.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance describes an efficiency-first approach for high-volume, straightforward, latency-sensitive, or cost-sensitive work: begin with a fast, low-cost model like Haiku, test thoroughly, and upgrade only when evals show a capability gap. Capability-first suits complex reasoning, not this case. Context window size isn't the deciding factor for short messages. Use-case-specific benchmark tests are called the most important step in choosing a model.

questions.question: Compliance requires that all model inference for one product's Claude API workspace runs only on US infrastructure. Several teams and ad-hoc scripts that never pass through CI use keys in that workspace, and the control must hold even when someone forgets a request parameter. What should the team configure?

options.text: Require every team to set the US inference region on each request and catch omissions in code review.
Add a CI lint rule that fails any build whose Claude API calls omit the US inference region parameter.
Rely on the workspace's data-storage region being US, since where data is stored sets where inference runs.
In the workspace settings, allow only the US inference region and make US the default for requests.

questions.explanation: Workspace settings can restrict which inference geos the workspace may use (requests naming another geo get an error) and set the default used when a request omits the parameter, which enforces the policy across every key in the workspace. Per-request discipline with code review fails the stated case of someone forgetting the parameter. A CI lint rule never sees scripts that bypass CI. Workspace geo controls data storage at rest and endpoint processing such as code execution, not where model inference runs.

questions.question: A European bank's policy requires that Claude inference stay within the EU. The architect notes that on the Claude API the inference_geo parameter currently offers only us and global. Which option satisfies the requirement?

options.text: Use Claude on Google Cloud through an EU multi-region or regional endpoint, accepting its pricing premium.
Use the Claude API with inference_geo set to global, since global routing prefers the region nearest the caller.
Use the Claude API and create a workspace whose workspace geo is set to the EU when the workspace is created.
Use the Amazon Bedrock global endpoint, which keeps traffic in the AWS account's home region.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud offers multi-region endpoints (us and eu) and regional endpoints that route data within a geography, at a 10% premium over global. That meets an EU-only requirement. On the Claude API, global may run inference in any geography, and us is the only workspace geo available. Bedrock's global endpoint routes dynamically across all regions, so it doesn't guarantee residency.

questions.question: An enterprise is moving a contract-review app to Claude in Amazon Bedrock so all data stays inside its AWS security boundary. Today the app uploads each contract once with the Files API and reuses it across several questions, and finance pulls daily spend from the Usage and Cost API, but neither is supported on this platform. Which TWO adjustments keep the app working inside the boundary? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Send each contract inline as document content and use prompt caching for the repeated contract prefix.
Upload contracts through the Claude API's Files API and pass the returned file IDs in Bedrock requests.
Send contract questions to the Claude API directly and keep Bedrock only for the app's other requests.
Track spend through the AWS account's native billing instead of the Usage and Cost API endpoints.
Point finance's daily spend job at the Bedrock endpoint's Usage and Cost path with an Admin API key.

questions.explanation: Claude in Amazon Bedrock supports the Messages API with prompt caching but not Files API inputs or the Usage and Cost endpoints, so contracts are sent inline with caching for the reused prefix, and spend comes from Bedrock's AWS-native billing. Uploading through the Claude API's Files API sends contracts outside the AWS boundary, and Files API inputs aren't supported on Bedrock anyway. Routing contract questions to the Claude API also breaks the boundary requirement. The Usage and Cost endpoints are listed as unsupported on this platform, so pointing a job at them won't work.
